name: Anticholinergic toxidrome
oneLiner: Hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter — and the bowel sounds are absent.
causativeAgents: antihistamines (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, promethazine)
tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) — also Na-channel toxicity
antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine)
atropine, hyoscine (scopolamine), glycopyrrolate
oxybutynin, tolterodine (urinary antimuscarinics)
plants: Datura stramonium (jimsonweed), Atropa belladonna, Brugmansia
differentialDiagnosis: sympathomimetic toxidrome (skin is sweaty, bowel sounds present)
serotonin syndrome (clonus + hyperreflexia, history of serotonergic agent)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG (TCA → wide QRS).
Cooling: undress, evaporative + tepid sponging; target core temp < 38.5°C.
IV fluid resuscitation (isotonic crystalloid) for hyperthermia / rhabdomyolysis prevention.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV titrated) for agitation — avoid antipsychotics (worsen anticholinergic load and lower seizure threshold).
Foley catheter for urinary retention if present.

Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV slowly (over 5 min) ONLY for pure anticholinergic delirium without TCA features and without ECG changes — contraindicated if QRS > 100 ms or any conduction delay. Discuss with toxicology first.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus if TCA overdose with wide QRS.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if presented within 1 hour AND airway protected.
antidote: Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV (adult) slowly — only in pure anticholinergic delirium with normal ECG; do not use if TCA suspected.
redFlags: QRS > 100 ms (TCA poisoning) — give sodium bicarbonate, urgent ICU.
Seizures — benzodiazepines first-line.
Core temp > 40°C — aggressive active cooling.
Rhabdomyolysis (CK rising, dark urine) — IV fluids + monitor K+ / renal function.

references.label: UK National Poisons Information Service / TOXBASE — anticholinergic poisoning

name: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE / DUMBELS)
oneLiner: Wet everywhere (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, GI cramps, emesis) with fasciculations and miosis — think organophosphate.

features.mentalStatus: anxiety → confusion → coma in severe cases
other: garlic / petroleum odour on patient or clothing

causativeAgents: organophosphate pesticides (malathion, chlorpyrifos, parathion, dichlorvos)
carbamate pesticides (carbaryl, methomyl, propoxur) — usually milder, self-limiting
nerve agents (sarin, VX, novichok)
medicinal cholinergics overdose (pyridostigmine, neostigmine, donepezil, rivastigmine)
muscarinic mushrooms (Inocybe spp., Clitocybe spp.)
differentialDiagnosis: opioid overdose (also miosis + respiratory depression, but skin is dry and no fasciculations)
pontine stroke (miosis + coma but no SLUDGE)
management: PPE for staff — organophosphate is dermally absorbed; remove patient's clothing, wash skin with copious soap & water before extensive resuscitation.
ABC; high-flow O₂; suction copious secretions; early intubation if airway / ventilation compromised. AVOID succinylcholine (prolonged paralysis — pseudocholinesterase already inhibited).

Atropine 1-3 mg IV (adult) or 0.05 mg/kg (child) — DOUBLE the dose every 3-5 minutes until secretions dry and chest is clear; titrate to bronchorrhoea, NOT to pupil size or heart rate. May need very large cumulative doses (tens to hundreds of mg).

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) 30 mg/kg IV over 30 min (max 2 g), then 8-10 mg/kg/h infusion — give within 24-48 h of exposure, before ageing of the enzyme. Carbamate poisoning does not strictly require pralidoxime.
Benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg IV) for seizures and to reduce CNS toxicity.
Continuous cardiac monitoring; manage hypotension with IV fluids and noradrenaline if needed.
antidote: Atropine (titrated to dry secretions — primary endpoint is clear chest, not heart rate) PLUS pralidoxime (2-PAM) for organophosphates.
redFlags: Bronchorrhoea / bronchospasm — main cause of death; aggressive atropine.
Respiratory muscle weakness — anticipate intubation; AVOID suxamethonium.
Seizures or coma — benzodiazepines, ICU.
Type II (intermediate) syndrome 1-4 days post-exposure: proximal weakness, cranial nerve palsies → may need re-ventilation.

references.label: WHO. The WHO recommended classification of pesticides by hazard.
Eddleston M et al. Management of acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning. Lancet 2008;371:597-607.

name: Opioid toxidrome
oneLiner: Triad: pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + depressed mental status — reverse with naloxone, titrate to ventilation not consciousness.

features.respiratoryRate: bradypnoea (< 12) or apnoea — the lethal feature
features.pupils: miosis (pinpoint) — may be normal in meperidine, tramadol, propoxyphene, polypharmacy or anoxic injury
other: track marks / patches / fentanyl analogue concerns

causativeAgents: heroin, fentanyl + analogues (carfentanil, nitazenes — extremely potent, may need repeat naloxone)
prescription opioids (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone, buprenorphine, tramadol)
loperamide (very high doses → QT prolongation + opioid features)
diphenoxylate-atropine (Lomotil — mixed opioid + anticholinergic features)
differentialDiagnosis: clonidine / imidazoline overdose (miosis + bradycardia, no rescue with naloxone)
organophosphate poisoning (also miosis, but wet and bradypnoeic with bronchorrhoea)
management: ABC — bag-mask ventilation with 100% O₂ first; this alone reverses most opioid deaths.

Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV (adult, opioid-tolerant) or 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/intranasal in non-tolerant overdose. Titrate to adequate ventilation (RR ≥ 12, SpO₂ ≥ 92%), NOT to full alertness — over-reversal precipitates withdrawal, agitation, vomiting + aspiration.
Repeat naloxone every 2-3 min; if > 10 mg needed without response, reconsider diagnosis.
Naloxone infusion 2/3 of the effective bolus per hour for long-acting agents (methadone, sustained-release oxycodone, fentanyl patch, nitazenes).
IV fluids + supportive care; consider intubation if no response to naloxone or refractory hypoxia / NCPE.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG only if recent ingestion AND protected airway.
Refer to addiction services; consider buprenorphine induction if patient is willing and meets criteria. Distribute take-home naloxone.
antidote: Naloxone — see opioid-naloxone record for full dosing protocol.
redFlags: Pulmonary oedema / NCPE — supportive ventilation, PEEP.
QT prolongation (methadone) — continuous cardiac monitoring.
Body packer / stuffer — whole-bowel irrigation, surgical consult.
Polypharmacy (especially benzodiazepines / alcohol) — full naloxone reversal still leaves ventilatory depression; do not discharge prematurely.
Synthetic opioid (fentanyl analogue / nitazene) suspected — expect re-sedation, longer monitoring (≥ 6 h post last dose).

references.label: WHO. Community management of opioid overdose. 2014.
Boyer EW. Management of opioid analgesic overdose. NEJM 2012;367:146-55.

name: Sympathomimetic toxidrome
oneLiner: Hyperadrenergic state: hypertension + tachycardia + hyperthermia + mydriasis + diaphoresis + agitation — skin is sweaty, bowel sounds present (distinguishes from anticholinergic).

features.bloodPressure: hypertension (may be severe; risk of intracranial bleed, aortic dissection)
features.bowelSounds: normal / hyperactive — KEY differentiator from anticholinergic (absent)

causativeAgents: cocaine (also Na-channel blockade → wide QRS)
amphetamines, methamphetamine, MDMA, MDPV (bath salts), cathinones
phenylpropanolamine, pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, phentermine
synthetic cannabinoids (variable presentation)
thyroid storm (clinical mimic — not a poisoning)
khat (Catha edulis) — cathinone-containing
differentialDiagnosis: anticholinergic toxidrome (dry skin, absent bowel sounds)
serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, history of serotonergic agent)
neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rigidity, history of antipsychotic exposure, slower onset)
management: ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, IV access, large-bore access for fluids.

Aggressive benzodiazepines (lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q5min titrated; or diazepam 5-10 mg IV q5min) — FIRST LINE for agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, and to lower body temperature indirectly. Cumulative doses often large.

Active cooling: undress, evaporative cooling, cool IV fluids; target core temp < 38.5°C within 30 min. Consider neuromuscular blockade + intubation + cooling if temp > 41°C refractory to benzodiazepines.
IV fluid resuscitation (isotonic crystalloid) for rhabdomyolysis prevention and hyperthermia.

Hypertension: titrate benzodiazepines first. If persistent, use vasodilator (phentolamine 1-5 mg IV; nitroglycerin or nicardipine infusion). AVOID pure β-blockers (esmolol, propranolol) in cocaine — historic concern of unopposed α-agonism; if β-blockade is required use a combined α/β agent (labetalol) only after α-blockade established.
Cocaine + chest pain: aspirin, nitroglycerin, benzodiazepines; if STEMI, primary PCI is preferred over thrombolysis.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV for QRS widening (cocaine Na-channel blockade).
antidote: No specific antidote. Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of management.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening; aggressive cooling + paralysis.
Wide QRS or ventricular arrhythmia (cocaine) — sodium bicarbonate.
Severe hypertension with end-organ damage — vasodilator, NOT pure β-blockade.
Chest pain — rule out MI / aortic dissection.
Seizures — benzodiazepines; if refractory, barbiturates or propofol.
Hyponatraemia (MDMA + free water) — careful sodium correction.

references.label: Richards JR et al. Treatment of cocaine cardiovascular toxicity. Clin Toxicol 2016.

name: Sedative-hypnotic toxidrome
oneLiner: CNS depression with relatively preserved vitals: somnolence + slurred speech + ataxia + nystagmus, normal pupils, normal-ish respirations (until severe).

features.respiratoryRate: normal early; bradypnoea in severe cases (especially with alcohol or opioid co-ingestion)
features.mentalStatus: drowsy → stupor → coma in overdose; ataxia, slurred speech, disinhibition
other: co-ingestion with alcohol is the main lethality multiplier

causativeAgents: benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, clonazepam, midazolam)
Z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone, eszopiclone)
barbiturates (phenobarbital, thiopental) — narrower therapeutic index, higher mortality
gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) and precursors (GBL, 1,4-BD)
ethanol (the most common co-ingestant)
first-generation antihistamines (also anticholinergic)
carisoprodol, meprobamate
differentialDiagnosis: opioid toxidrome (miosis + bradypnoea; reverses with naloxone)
management: ABC, supplemental O₂, IV access, glucose check (POC + lab), continuous cardiac + pulse-oximetry monitoring.
Supportive care is the mainstay — most patients do well with airway protection and observation.
Bag-mask ventilation / intubation for inadequate ventilation, hypoxia, or loss of airway reflexes.
IV fluids for hypotension; vasopressors rarely needed.

Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV (then 0.3-0.5 mg q1min, max 3 mg) for ISOLATED iatrogenic benzodiazepine over-sedation in a benzodiazepine-naive patient. AVOID in chronic benzodiazepine users, mixed overdose (especially with TCAs), known seizure disorder — risk of refractory seizures.
Active rewarming if hypothermic.
Consider haemodialysis for severe phenobarbital or carbamazepine overdose.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if presented < 1 h AND airway protected.
antidote: Flumazenil — for isolated, iatrogenic benzodiazepine over-sedation only. Do NOT use empirically in mixed or chronic-user overdose.
redFlags: Mixed overdose with opioids, alcohol, or TCAs — disproportionate respiratory failure.
Severe barbiturate poisoning — coma, hypothermia, hypotension → ICU + consider haemodialysis (phenobarbital).
GHB overdose — abrupt awakening 2-4 h later; do not assume malingering.
Aspiration pneumonia.

references.label: Penninga EI et al. Adverse events associated with flumazenil treatment. BMC Pharmacol Toxicol 2016.

name: Serotonin syndrome
oneLiner: Triad: mental status change + autonomic hyperactivity + neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia — LOWER-LIMB DOMINANT). Hunter Criteria > Sternbach.

features.mentalStatus: agitation, restlessness, confusion → coma in severe cases
other: clonus — spontaneous, inducible (ankle) or ocular — KEY finding

causativeAgents: SSRIs / SNRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine)
MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, moclobemide) — high-risk combinations
tramadol, tapentadol, meperidine, fentanyl, methadone, pethidine
ondansetron, metoclopramide, dextromethorphan, linezolid (also MAOI activity)
St John's wort, MDMA, cocaine, amphetamines, LSD
lithium, triptans (combined with SSRIs)
methylene blue (MAOI activity) given to a patient on SSRI
differentialDiagnosis: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (slow onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, normo- or hyporeflexia, history of antipsychotic exposure)
management: Stop all serotonergic agents IMMEDIATELY — most cases resolve within 24 h once the offending agent is withdrawn.
ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, IV fluids.
Aggressive cooling for hyperthermia: undress, evaporative cooling, IV crystalloid; target core temp < 38.5°C.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV q5min titrated; or diazepam) for agitation, tremor, clonus — first line. Cumulative doses often large.

Cyproheptadine PO/NG — 12 mg loading dose, then 2 mg q2h while symptoms persist, up to 8 mg q6h maintenance (max 32 mg/24 h). Limited evidence; reasonable in moderate-severe cases unresponsive to benzodiazepines. No IV form.

Severe / refractory hyperthermia (> 41°C) — intubation + non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade (rocuronium / vecuronium — AVOID succinylcholine, exacerbates hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis) + active cooling + sedation.
Manage hypertension as for sympathomimetic; AVOID propranolol (long-acting, masks tachycardia which is a useful clinical marker).
Treat rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids), monitor renal function, K+, lactate, CK.
antidote: Cyproheptadine PO/NG (5-HT2A antagonist) — adjunct to benzodiazepines + supportive care in moderate-severe cases.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening; intubation, paralysis, aggressive cooling.
Rigidity with rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC.
Seizures — benzodiazepines.
Recent linezolid or methylene blue exposure — high index of suspicion.
Mixed with MDMA — also risk hyponatraemia from free-water intake.

references.label: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. NEJM 2005;352:1112-20.
Dunkley EJC et al. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. QJM 2003;96:635-42.

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
oneLiner: Tetrad over hours-to-days: lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + altered mental status, after dopamine antagonist exposure or dopaminergic withdrawal.
causativeAgents: typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine) — highest risk
atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine) — lower risk but possible
antiemetics with dopamine antagonism (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol)
abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic agents (levodopa, amantadine, pramipexole) in Parkinson's patients — 'parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome'
lithium, tetrabenazine
differentialDiagnosis: serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, clonus + hyperreflexia, lower-limb dominant)
malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic trigger; hypercarbia; succinylcholine / volatile anaesthetic)
management: STOP the offending dopamine antagonist immediately. If parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia, RESTART the withdrawn dopaminergic agent.
ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, large-bore IV fluids — high-volume to support renal perfusion (myoglobinuric AKI risk).
Aggressive active cooling: undress, evaporative cooling, cool IV fluids; target core temp < 38.5°C.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV q4-6h) — first-line for agitation, mild-moderate cases.
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO/NG q6-8h titrated up to 5 mg q4-6h (max 40 mg/day) — dopamine agonist, restores dopaminergic tone. Onset 24-72 h.
Dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6h (max 10 mg/kg/day) — direct muscle relaxant; reserve for severe rigidity / hyperthermia. Beware hepatotoxicity.
Amantadine 100 mg PO/NG bd as alternative dopaminergic agent.
Severe / refractory — intubation + non-depolarising paralysis + ICU. ECT has been used for refractory NMS and lethal catatonia.
Monitor CK, K+, lactate, renal function, coags; treat rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids, ± urinary alkalinisation).
DVT prophylaxis early — high VTE risk from immobility + rigidity.
Avoid antipsychotic re-challenge for at least 2 weeks after recovery; if needed later, use a different class at the lowest effective dose.
antidote: Bromocriptine PO (dopamine agonist) + dantrolene IV (muscle relaxant) for moderate-severe disease, in addition to withdrawal of the offending agent.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening, ICU.
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric AKI — aggressive IV fluids, renal replacement if needed.
Severe rigidity — risk of compartment syndrome.
Aspiration, pulmonary embolism (immobility), DIC.
Recurrence on re-introduction of antipsychotic — wait ≥ 2 weeks and use a different class.

references.label: Strawn JR et al. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Am J Psychiatry 2007;164:870-6.
Berman BD. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: a review for neurohospitalists. Neurohospitalist 2011;1:41-7.

name: Salicylate toxicity
oneLiner: Mixed primary respiratory alkalosis + primary metabolic acidosis with tinnitus, hyperpnoea (Kussmaul-like), nausea, agitation, hyperthermia — even at therapeutic levels in chronic toxicity.

features.respiratoryRate: tachypnoea + hyperpnoea (deep) — drives the respiratory alkalosis
features.mentalStatus: agitation → confusion → coma in severe / chronic poisoning
features.bowelSounds: normal or hyperactive; nausea, vomiting, haematemesis
other: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema in severe cases
anion-gap metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory alkalosis

causativeAgents: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
topical methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen, deep heat rubs) — 1 tsp = ~7 g aspirin equivalent; lethal in children
bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) — chronic, in children
salicylate-containing keratolytics (high concentration over large body surface area)
differentialDiagnosis: DKA (high anion gap, but glucose elevated and ketones present)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac + pulse-oximetry monitoring, serial salicylate levels (q2h until peak then q4h; consider extended-release / enteric-coated formulations may peak late).
Salicylate level (mg/dL) + ABG + electrolytes + glucose + renal/liver function + lactate + coagulation + CK.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG within 1-2 h of acute ingestion (multiple-dose may be considered for sustained-release / massive ingestion).
IV fluid resuscitation (D5W with potassium added once urine output established) — patients are profoundly dehydrated.

SODIUM BICARBONATE IV — 1-2 mEq/kg bolus, then infusion (150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1 L D5W at 1.5-2 × maintenance) — target urine pH > 7.5 and serum pH 7.45-7.55. Maintains salicylate in ionised form (ion trapping), enhances renal excretion, reverses CNS acidosis.
POTASSIUM REPLETION is essential — hypokalaemia prevents urinary alkalinisation. Aim for K+ 4-4.5 mmol/L.
Glucose — give D50 boluses even if serum glucose normal (CNS hypoglycaemia despite normal serum levels).

HAEMODIALYSIS — indications include level > 100 mg/dL acute (> 90 in chronic), altered mental status, renal failure, severe acid-base disturbance, pulmonary or cerebral oedema, or refractory to alkalinisation.
antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is alkalinisation (sodium bicarbonate + potassium repletion) and early haemodialysis for severe poisoning.
redFlags: Altered mental status — INDICATION FOR HAEMODIALYSIS regardless of level.
Salicylate level > 100 mg/dL (acute) or > 60-90 mg/dL (chronic, often more toxic at lower level).
Cerebral oedema, seizures, coma.

Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — supportive ventilation; mechanical ventilation is HIGH-RISK as iatrogenic respiratory acidosis worsens CNS salicylate uptake. If intubation unavoidable, ventilate to match the patient's pre-intubation minute ventilation (often very high), give NaHCO₃ first.
Co-ingestion (paracetamol common with aspirin combination products).
Chronic toxicity in elderly — often missed, presents as confusion / acidosis.

references.label: EXTRIP workgroup. Extracorporeal treatment for salicylate poisoning. Ann Emerg Med 2015;66:165-81.
